title: evaluate() doesn't work for code using `srcref` or `wholeSrcref`
description:
`evaluate()` doesn't work if the evaluated code uses the `srcref` (or `wholeSrcref`) attribute (most likely because `parse_all()` removes these attributes from the expressions). Consider for example the following code from [Advanced R](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/functions.html?q=srcref#fun-components):
```
f02 <- function(x, y) {
  # A comment
  x + y
}
attr(f02, "srcref")
```
In the console it produces
```
> f02 <- function(x, y) {
+     # A comment
+     x + y
+ }
> attr(f02, "srcref")
function(x, y) {
    # A comment
    x + y
}
```
However,
```
evaluate("f02 <- function(x, y) {
  # A comment
  x + y
}
attr(f02, \"srcref\")")
```
produces
```
> evaluate("f02 <- function(x, y) {
+   # A comment
+   x + y
+ }
+ attr(f02, \"srcref\")")
<evaluation>
Source code: 
  f02 <- function(x, y) {
    # A comment
    x + y
  }
Source code: 
  attr(f02, "srcref")
Text output: 
  NULL
```
Due to this the example in "Advanced R" and many examples in the vignettes of the package I'm currently working on are not displayed correctly.

Is it possible to update `parse_all()` such that the srcref attributes (`srcref`, `srcfile`, `wholeSrcref`) are preserved.

title: new evaluate does remove identical plot more aggressively
description:
This was reported in 
- https://github.com/quarto-dev/quarto-cli/discussions/12707

Previously, with 0.24.0, this would produce two recorded plot

``` r
ev <- evaluate::evaluate(function() {
     hist(cars$speed)
     hist(cars$speed, breaks = "Scott")
 })
 lapply(ev, class)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "source"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "recordedplot"
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] "source"
#> 
#> [[4]]
#> [1] "recordedplot"
 packageVersion("evaluate")
#> [1] '0.24.0'
```

and **knitr** would be responsible to keep only one or all depending on `fig.keep` options

````r
> md <- glue::glue("
```{r}
hist(cars$speed)
hist(cars$speed, breaks = 'Scott')
```
", .open = "{{", .close = "}}")
> knitr::knit(text = md) |> cat()
1/1 [unnamed-chunk-1]

``` r
hist(cars$speed)
hist(cars$speed, breaks = 'Scott')
```

![plot of chunk unnamed-chunk-1](figure/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png)

> knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.keep="all")
> knitr::knit(text = md) |> cat()
1/1 [unnamed-chunk-1]

``` r
hist(cars$speed)
```

![plot of chunk unnamed-chunk-1](figure/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png)

``` r
hist(cars$speed, breaks = 'Scott')
```

![plot of chunk unnamed-chunk-1](figure/unnamed-chunk-1-2.png)
````

However, with **evaluate** 1.0.0, there is now a new logic to detect different plots 

``` r
evaluate::evaluate(function() {
     hist(cars$speed)
     hist(cars$speed, breaks = "Scott")
 })
#> <evaluation>
#> Source code: 
#>   hist(cars$speed)
#> Plot [7]:
#>   <base> C_plot_new()
#>   <base> palette2()
#>   <base> C_plot_window()
#>   <base> C_title()
#>   <base> C_axis()
#>   <base> C_axis()
#>   <base> C_rect()
#> Source code: 
#>   hist(cars$speed, breaks = "Scott")
```


So `fig.keep = 'all'` does not have the effect as there is no second plot to keep now. 

Is this change expected?

Or could it be something to check when this was rewritten ?  

https://github.com/r-lib/evaluate/blob/1c4492bcb229a094286a8c1af5a8172c35017809/R/watchout.R#L62-L69

title: Hooks left in place after time limit error
description:
This example was posted [on stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/q/79594532).  If the document

````

```{r}
ans <- 6 * 7
Sys.sleep(2)
```

Answer: `r ans`
````

is saved in `timeout.Rmd` and then this code is run you get weird results, because the plot hooks have been left in place:
```
setTimeLimit(elapsed = 1)       # set a timeout
knitr::knit("timeout.Rmd")      # knit the document which triggers it 
print(1)                        # this works, but the hooks are still there
plot(1)                         # this triggers them
print(1)                        # Now this doesn't appear
```

There's some variability in the results:  RStudio seems to be okay (I guess it is restoring the hooks after the plot).  Calling `getHook("before.plot.new")` after the `knit()` call sometimes shows the hook, sometimes doesn't. 

I haven't been able to put together an example that doesn't involve `knitr::knit()`.  Simple calls to `evaluate()` don't have the issue.

title: Negative side effects from always recording examples with `pdf(NULL)`
description:
I'm observing some negative side effects in certain `{pkgdown}` examples that seem to stem from the decision in `{evaluate}` v1.0 to always use `pdf(NULL)` to **record** graphical examples instead of `getOption("device")` which `{pkgdown}` sets to `ragg::agg_png()`:

* https://github.com/r-lib/pkgdown/issues/2874
* https://github.com/r-lib/pkgdown/issues/2878
* Reprex: https://github.com/trevorld/pkgdown.pdf.null.reprex

I observe these problems go away if I manually **downgrade** `{evaluate}` to v0.24.0 with `remotes::install_github("r-lib/evaluate", "v0.24.0")`.

I speculate that the new `ragg::agg_record()` device in the developmental version of `{ragg}` may be a better choice of device than `pdf(NULL)` (once released).

Some references to the `pdf(NULL` change that was made here:

- https://github.com/r-lib/evaluate/blob/9b412235d0d8a804603637ccecff98e880003feb/R/watchout.R#L9
- https://github.com/r-lib/evaluate/commit/c750df44483c76ac18b397ff27361aa7b38650b1
- https://github.com/r-lib/evaluate/pull/132

title: Can't set `rlang_trace_top_env` for expected errors
description:
This affects testthat snapshots in particular, see what happens to rlang backtrace tests with dev evaluate:

https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/compare/tmp/evaluate-snapshots?expand=1

I don't see a way of accommodating `rlang_trace_top_env` with the new evaluation setup. Possible solutions:

1. Revert the new evaluation scheme and give up on `on.exit`.

2. Add an option to trim rlang backtraces to `evaluate()`, following the approach discussed in https://github.com/r-lib/evaluate/issues/220:
    - Insert a dummy frame on the stack to serve as sentinel
    - Add a variant of `rlang_trace_top_env` on rlang that indicates the _parent_ of the top env. This would be set to the dummy frame.
  
    If this new argument if off by default, this not only requires a release of rlang prior to releasing evaluate, but also releases of knitr and testthat once evaluate is on CRAN to use the new argument. But we can probably make it the default.

title: Regression with `last_error()` in knitr
description:
There's the issue of unexpected errors, as in #214, and there's also the issue of expected errors.

For unexpected errors, having the evaluate machinery as part of the backtrace is not a regression, as long as we also get the user stack in the backtrace. For expected errors though, we are not supposed to get the knitr stack:

CRAN:

````md

``` r
f <- function() g()
g <- function() h()
h <- function() i()
i <- function() rlang::abort('hop')
f()
```

```
## Error in `i()`:
## ! hop
```


``` r
rlang::last_error()
```

```
## <error/rlang_error>
## Error in `i()`:
## ! hop
## ---
## Backtrace:
##     ▆
##  1. └─global f()
##  2.   └─global g()
##  3.     └─global h()
##  4.       └─global i()
## Run ]8;;x-r-run:rlang::last_trace(drop = FALSE)rlang::last_trace(drop = FALSE)]8;; to see 1 hidden frame.
```
````

dev:

````md
``` r
f <- function() g()
g <- function() h()
h <- function() i()
i <- function() rlang::abort('hop')
f()
```

```
## Error in `i()`:
## ! hop
```


``` r
rlang::last_error()
```

```
## <error/rlang_error>
## Error in `i()`:
## ! hop
## ---
## Backtrace:
##      ▆
##   1. ├─evaluate (local) `<fn>`()
##   2. │ ├─base::withRestarts(...) at ]8;line = 144:col = 7;file:///Users/lionel/Sync/Projects/R/r-lib/evaluate/R/evaluate.Revaluate/R/evaluate.R:144:7]8;;
##   3. │ │ └─base (local) withRestartList(expr, restarts)
##   4. │ │   ├─base (local) withOneRestart(withRestartList(expr, restarts[-nr]), restarts[[nr]])
##   5. │ │   │ └─base (local) doWithOneRestart(return(expr), restart)
##   6. │ │   └─base (local) withRestartList(expr, restarts[-nr])
##   7. │ │     ├─base (local) withOneRestart(withRestartList(expr, restarts[-nr]), restarts[[nr]])
##   8. │ │     │ └─base (local) doWithOneRestart(return(expr), restart)
##   9. │ │     └─base (local) withRestartList(expr, restarts[-nr])
##  10. │ │       └─base (local) withOneRestart(expr, restarts[[1L]])
##  11. │ │         └─base (local) doWithOneRestart(return(expr), restart)
##  12. │ ├─evaluate:::with_handlers(...)
##  13. │ │ ├─base::eval(call) at ]8;line = 51:col = 3;file:///Users/lionel/Sync/Projects/R/r-lib/evaluate/R/conditions.Revaluate/R/conditions.R:51:3]8;;
##  14. │ │ │ └─base::eval(call)
##  15. │ │ └─base::withCallingHandlers(...)
##  16. │ └─base::withVisible(do) at ]8;line = 153:col = 15;file:///Users/lionel/Sync/Projects/R/r-lib/evaluate/R/evaluate.Revaluate/R/evaluate.R:153:15]8;;
##  17. └─global f()
##  18.   └─global g()
##  19.     └─global h()
##  20.       └─global i()
## Run ]8;;x-r-run:rlang::last_trace(drop = FALSE)rlang::last_trace(drop = FALSE)]8;; to see 1 hidden frame.
```
````

To fix this we need to work around how rlang trims the backtrace in [trace_trim_env_idx](https://github.com/r-lib/rlang/blob/69659c49cc2b58bc68755693deaa2f271efadbc6/R/trace.R#L604):

```r
  to <- to %||% peek_option("rlang_trace_top_env")

  # Trim knitr context if available
  if (is_null(to) && is_true(peek_option('knitr.in.progress'))) {
    to <- knitr::knit_global()
  }
```

The `knit_global()` environment is no longer correct here because it refers to the frame environment where we now register on-exit expressions. It seems like we could solve this by setting `rlang_trace_top_env` to a new environment inserted on the stack just for this purpose. The problem is that this would need to be an exclusive boundary rather than an inclusive one, which would require changes in rlang, such as a new `rlang_trace_top_env_exclusive` or `rlang_trace_top_env_parent` option.

`evaluate()` could optionally set the top-env to that dummy stack frame, this way it's easy to set in more contexts than just knitr.

Reason for increasing the required R version to >= 4.0?
description:
Hello, I see that the required R version has been bumped from 3.0.2 to 4.0 in https://github.com/r-lib/evaluate/pull/128. I'm wondering what is the reason behind this change. 

I understand that the `tidyverse` policy is to support the previous 4 versions, meaning back to 4.0 at the time of writing. However, AFAIK `evaluate` is not part of the `tidyverse` and is not listed in `tidyverse::tidyverse_deps()`. Also, while one can choose to use alternatives to the `tidyverse` packages for data wrangling, `r-lib` packages are the foundation for many tools used across a large number of packages, e.g. `testthat`, `knitr`. With this change, no package can run `testthat` on versions < 4.0 anymore.

So unless this change is motivated by technical reasons (which doesn't seem to be the case based on the changes in #128), wouldn't it be better to keep the required R version as low as possible? 

Finally, I didn't see any announcements on this quite important change and this is also not mentioned in NEWS. Having some information on this and some explanation of the consequences would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks

title: Rmd file does not respect options()$warn across chunks
description:
Hello,

There seems to be an issue in how the `warning` option is handled inside an Rmd file.
This relates to an earlier pull request https://github.com/r-lib/evaluate/pull/81#issue-251835531 and the original issue on https://github.com/yihui/knitr/issues/1425#issue-251433392

The `warn` option does not correctly persist across the Rmd file chunks.

Here is an example code to test the behaviour:

    ```{r pt1}
    f <- function(x) {warning("Warning raised!"); x}

    options(warn = 0)
    options()$warn
    f(TRUE)
    ```

    ```{r pt2}
    options(warn = 1)
    options()$warn
    f(TRUE)

    options(warn = 2)
    ```

    ```{r ops-fail}
    options()$warn
    f(TRUE)
    ```

Last `options()$warn` reports value of `1`, and thus the last call to `f()` does not raise an error, even though the option was explicitly set in the previous code chunk.

I hope this is helpful.

title: plot handler called too late when evaluating a loop
description:
In the IRkernel, we [encountered a problem were we couldn't explain the order of the output of a evaluated loop](https://github.com/IRkernel/IRkernel/issues/295). The situation is basically this:

``` R
library(evaluate)

code <- "
for (i in 1:5) {
txt(paste('call:', i),'call')
cars <- c(i, 3, 6, 4, 9)
plot(cars)   
}
"

l <- list()
txt <- function(o, type) {
  t <- paste(o, collapse = '\n')
  l[length(l)+1] <<- t
}
oh <- new_output_handler(source = identity, 
                         text = function(o) txt(o, "text"), 
                         graphics = function(o) txt("plot", "plot"),
                         message = identity, 
                         warning = identity, 
                         error = identity, 
                         value = identity)


x <- evaluate(code, output_handler = oh)
cat(paste(l, collapse="\n"))
```

-> The resulting list is both filled by the handler and by a call from the evaluated code.

The problem is that it seems that the in some cases, the call happens too early:

```
> cat(paste(l, collapse="\n"))
call: 1               # No plot has triggered the handler -> call is first
call: 2               # second loop ...
plot                  # but the plot from the first loop is only now being handled
call: 3               # again a too early call
plot                  # plot from the second loop
call: 4
plot
call: 5
plot
plot
```

When "unrolling" the loop, it looks fine:

``` R
code <- "
{i <- 1
txt(paste('call:', i),'call')
cars <- c(i, 3, 6, 4, 9)
plot(cars)   
}
{i <- 2
txt(paste('call:', i),'call')
cars <- c(i, 3, 6, 4, 9)
plot(cars)   
}
{i <- 3
txt(paste('call:', i),'call')
cars <- c(i, 3, 6, 4, 9)
plot(cars)   
}
# [...]
"
```

```
> cat(paste(l, collapse="\n"))
call: 1
plot
call: 2
plot
call: 3
plot
# [...]
```

Any idea why this happens and if there is any way to get this in the right order?

title: Use correct encoding
description:
on windows, to correctly parse text, you need to do:

``` r
parse(text = code, encoding = Encoding(code))
```

if the `code` has set an encoding, it gets returned by `Encoding`. Else, `Encoding` returns `'unknown'`, the default value for `encoding` in `parse`.

ideally, `parse_all` should internally do the above instead of a `encoding`-less `parse` call.

an alternative would be to pass down an `encoding` parameter through `evaluate` → `parse_all` → `parse`

title: flush.console does not trigger a handle_output
description:
Currently handle_output is only triggered when either a expression is finished evaluating or `message/...` is called in the evaluated code. This leads to the situation that when you evaluate a long-running loop, no output is sent until the loop is complete, even when calling `flush.console` or `flush(stdout())`. 

In [irkernel](https://github.com/IRkernel/IRkernel/issues/3), this means that you only get the output of a loop after the loop is complete, which might be seconds or hours... A current workaround is calling `message(..)` instead of `print(...)`, which both shows the message immediately and also the up-to-then output thanks to the call to handle_output during the message handling.

Would it be possible to add a way to overwrite `flush_console` and `flush` with functions which first call the "real" functions and then `handle_output`? this would give users a way to trigger sending the output...

```
> xxx <- flush.console
> flush.console <- function(){xxx();print("flushing")}
> flush.console()
[1] "flushing"
```

Code to test the problem:

```
library(evaluate)

code <- "for (i in 1:5){
print(\"text\")
message('message')
Sys.sleep(1)
}
print(\"break\")
for (i in 1:5){
  print(\"text\")
  Sys.sleep(1)
}"


l = list()
txt <- function(o, type) {
  t <- paste(o, collapse = '\n')
  t <- paste("OUT: ", t)
  l[length(l)+1] <<- paste("T: ",Sys.time()," type: ", type, "  -> ", t)
}
oh <- new_output_handler(source = identity, 
                         text = function(o) txt(o, "text"), 
                         graphics = identity,
                         message = function(o) txt(o, "message"), 
                         warning = function(o) txt(o, "warn"), 
                         error = function(o) txt(o, "error"), 
                         value = identity)



x <- evaluate(code, output_handler = oh)
l
```

I can sent a PR which does just that: if evaluate gets a parameter to `flush`, it will overwrite these two function in the env which is passed to eval, do the eval and remove these two references again.

title: Multibyte characters in source code
description:
(Originally reported at yihui/knitr#988) When there are multibyte characters in the source code, `parse_all()` fails to extract the correct source:

``` r

#               src        expr
```

This is because `srcref` gives the column positions based on _bytes_ instead of column numbers (characters), e.g. the first example above has an expression from the 1st to 7th byte. title: bug when evaluating code containing quoted multi-byte characters
description:
I noticed this since the beginning of `knitr`, but have not tracked down to the real problem until today. It may well be a bug of R in `srcfilecopy`, but that is too deep for me to go, and I have found a fix in `evaluate`, so I'm not going to bother R core.

This bug might be difficult for you to reproduce; it only happens under Windows:

``` r
> library(evaluate)
> parse_all(c('1+1', '"你好"'))
                 src  expr
0              1+1\n 1 + 1
1 "你<e5><U+00A5>&\b  你好
```

Note the second Chinese character `好` with the double quote `"` were ruined somehow in `src`. In theory we should get the results like this

``` r
>  parse_all(c('1+1','"你好"'))
     src  expr
0  1+1\n 1 + 1
1 "你好"  你好
```

I'll send you a pull request in a minute.
